claim: Early life adversity (ELA) is associated with increased risk for stress-related disorders later in life.
source: Early life adversity (ELA) is associated with increased risk for stress-related disorders later in life.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research establishing this relationship.

claim: ELA increases the lifetime risk for multiple forms of psychopathology, including anxiety disorders and major depressive disorder.
source: Early life adversity (ELA) increases the lifetime risk for multiple forms of psychopathology, including anxiety disorders and major depressive disorder (Agid et al., 1999; Draijer and Langeland, 1999; Heim and Nemeroff, 2001; Koenen and Widom, 2009; Widom, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: ELA is associated with higher rates of negative outcomes than similar events experienced in adulthood.
source: ELA is associated with higher rates of negative outcomes than similar events experienced in adulthood (Felitti et al., 1998; Heim and Nemeroff, 2001; McCauley et al., 1997; Mullen et al., 1996; Salmon and Bryant, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: ELA has been shown to drive early engagement of the basolateral amygdala (BLA), a key node supporting emotional processing, threat assessment, and fear learning.
source: In agreement with this prediction, ELA has been shown to drive early engagement of the basolateral amygdala (BLA), a key node supporting emotional processing, threat assessment, and fear learning (Bath et al., 2016; Moriceau et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The prelimbic (PL) subregion of the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) projects to the BLA and is necessary for fear retrieval.
source: Numerous studies have shown that the prelimbic (PL) subregion of the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) projects to the BLA (Do-Monte et al., 2015b; Vertes, 2004) and is necessary for fear retrieval (Burgos-Robles et al., 2009; Courtin et al., 2014; Sierra-Mercado et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The infralimbic (IL) subregion of mPFC supports extinction learning.
source: whereas the infralimbic (IL) subregion of mPFC supports extinction learning (Adhikari et al., 2015; Do-Monte et al., 2015a; Sierra-Mercado et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: PL projections into amygdala begin to emerge around postnatal day (PND) 7, increasing through adolescence.
source: Over early development, PL projections into amygdala begin to emerge around postnatal day (PND) 7, increasing through adolescence (Cunningham et al., 2002), and being pruned back during early adulthood (Bouwmeester et al., 2002; Cressman et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The infant PL, unlike adult PL, is not involved in the expression of sustained fear responses.
source: The relatively late integration of the PL into the threat learning circuit may explain recent reports suggesting that the infant PL, unlike adult PL, is not involved in the expression of sustained fear responses (Chan et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research and inference from developmental data.

evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: LB delays developmental processes such as sexual maturation and physical growth.
source: and delay developmental processes such as sexual maturation and physical growth (Manzano Nieves et al., 2019; Yam et al., 2017).

claim: LB impacts behavioral outcomes with effects that persist into adulthood, increasing depressive-like behaviors.

evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: LB alters behavioral response to stress.
source: altering behavioral response to stress (Cohen et al., 2013; Manzano-Nieves et al., 2018)

claim: LB affects hippocampal-dependent learning.
source: and affecting hippocampal-dependent learning (Bath et al., 2016; Bath et al., 2017; Manzano-Nieves et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2011).

claim: LB resulted in decreased body weight and brain weight from infancy into pre-adolescence.

source: LB males had decreased brain weight when compared to control males at PND 16, 21, and 28, with differences resolved by PND 35 (Figure 1C bottom).

claim: LB increased PV-positive cell density in the BLA at PND 21.
source: Using immunohistochemistry, we labeled PV-positive interneurons, a late differentiating subclass of inhibitory interneurons (Bartolini et al., 2013; Mukhopadhyay et al., 2009; Rymar and Sadikot, 2007), in the brain of LB and control reared male mice at PND 16, 21, 28, 50, and 75. PV-positive interneurons are known to begin differentiating between PND 10–28, reaching a mature phenotype at approximately PND 30 (Berdel and Moryś, 2000; Dávila et al., 2008). In BLA, LB led to an increased PV-positive cell density at PND 21 when compared to control reared mice at this age (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: No differences in PV-positive cell density was observed at PND 16 in BLA, with both groups expressing low densities of PV-positive cells.
source: No differences in PV-positive cell density was observed at PND 16, with both groups expressing low densities of PV-positive cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: The difference in PV-positive cell density between LB and control groups subsided by PND 28, with control PV-positive cell density rising to match those observed in LB mice.

evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4A.

evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4A.

source: A non-significant decrease in PV-positive cell density in LB mice was observed at PND 50 in BLA, IL, and PL.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4A.

evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.
